newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: G7 envoys meet Cambodia's PMs as Albright cancels.
newsitem.headline: G7 envoys meet Cambodia's PMs as Albright cancels.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright cancelled a trip to Cambodia because of security fears and special envoys from the Group of Seven told the country's feuding premiers of its concern about political stability.

Albright cancelled her trip because Cambodia's security situation was "serious and unpredictable", U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters on board Albright's plane en route to Hanoi where it landed on Thursday.

The two G7 envoys, Claude Martin, the French Foreign Ministry's Deputy Secretary General, and Yukio Imagawa, a former Japanese ambassador in Phnom Penh, had separate meetings on Thursday with both First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh and Second Prime Minister Hun Sen.

"We reported to the prime minister. The message is clear," said Shohei Naito, Japan's current ambassador to Cambodia, who took part in the talks. "It is the statement of the G8," he said, referring to the G7 and Russia.

The envoys did not talk to reporters but aides of the two prime ministers, who head a fractured coalition government, said both had assured the envoys that they would work towards resolving their differences.

The G7 leaders, who met with Russian President Boris Yeltsin in Denver last weekend, called for an end to Cambodia's political chaos and violence, which they said threatened to shatter the relative stability since U.N.-sponsored elections in 1993.

Political tension resulted last week in a battle on the streets of Phnom Penh between bodyguards loyal to the two prime ministers. The disintegrating Khmer Rouge guerrilla force has also become a key issue of contention between the two with both men seeking political advantage as the group splits up.
The G7 also urged Ranariddh and Hun Sen to demonstrate their commitment to democracy by setting a date for the next elections.
"The first prime minister said all their concerns are real and he shared their concerns," the chief of Ranariddh's cabinet, Ly Thuch, told reporters after Ranariddh met the envoys.
"He committed to work for Cambodia with the second prime minister...to resolve the exisiting crisis," Ly Thuch said.
Ly Thuch said Ranariddh had been able to tell the envoys that he and Hun Sen had agreed that Cambodia's next election would be on May 23.
Hun Sen spokesman Om Yentieng told reporters the second prime minister had assured the envoys he would work with Ranariddh to pass electoral laws and other legislation ahead of the polls.

Ranariddh's royalist party won the 1993 election but agreed to form the coalition with Hun Sen after he objected to the election results. Hun Sen led the communist government which ruled the country prior to the peace process.
Ly Thuch said Ranariddh had informed the envoys about the Khmer Rouge situation and told them the government was in the process of ending the civil war.
Ranariddh said earlier on Thursday there was no fresh news on the fate of Khmer Rouge leader Pol Pot who has reportedly been captured by a guerrilla faction which rebelled against him.
Pol Pot, mastermind of the Khmer Rouge's 1975-79 "killing fields" reign of terror, had to give him up to authorities if it wanted to make an amnesty deal with the government, he said.
